changes.before: If the context deadline is already in the past, what does this fake transaction report?
changes.after: Set a time limit on a request and check the outcome.

before:
http.Client delegates a single transaction to its RoundTripper. This fake transport returns an in-memory response and never calls the default transport, DNS, a listener or a socket. io.NopCloser wraps the strings.Reader with a Close method that does nothing; it does not acquire or release an external resource. Its RoundTrip checks the request context. Real custom transports must also honor cancellation during their actual blocking work.

request.Context() takes no arguments and returns the context attached to that request. Calling Err on that returned context observes whether cancellation or a deadline has already ended it; it does not create a new context.

NewRequestWithContext attaches the context; a one-hour timeout here is a bound, not a timing assertion. Defer cancel releases context resources. On successful Do, close the response body even when reading fails. A received HTTP error status is not automatically a Do transport error; inspect StatusCode separately. The fixture reads only its known tiny in-memory body.

io.ReadAll receives the response body as a Reader, consumes its remaining bytes and returns a byte slice plus an error. It can allocate for all remaining input, so this example deliberately supplies only its known tiny body.
Expected output or behavior: 200 ready. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Explain why this fake proves control flow but not real-network timeout reliability or security. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A transport handles one request and its reply for an HTTP client. This fake transport does all its work in memory. It checks `request.Context().Err()` to see whether the request has already been stopped. No network connection is opened.

A deadline is the latest time work should continue. This context allows up to one hour; it does not wait an hour. The request carries that context. If a response arrives, read and close its body and check both errors. A response status, such as 404, is separate from a transport error.
The screen shows `200 ready`. The fake response has status 200 and the text ready. Its body can be closed without releasing a real network connection.
If the deadline already passed, the error path checks for DeadlineExceeded using errors.Is. This tests the program's handling of that result, not the timing of a real network.
